title: AI forward deployed engineer
summary: A curated sequence over the library for a AI forward deployed engineer: 34 lessons in 8 modules, from the foundations of the role to its advanced topics.

modules.title: Foundations: The Forward Deployed Delivery Model
modules.intro: This module covers how a forward deployed engineer takes a customer engagement from a signed scope to a system running in production, and the working methods that keep that delivery bounded and verifiable. It moves from the delivery model itself to scoping and design documents, workflow mapping, and proofs of concept with measurable exit criteria.

modules.title: Software Foundations for Field Engineering
modules.intro: A forward deployed engineer writes most of the glue between a customer's systems and an AI product, usually alone and under time pressure, so the general-purpose stack has to be second nature. This module covers the five foundations that work rests on: Python, TypeScript on Node.js, React with Next.js, Postgres, and AI coding tools used with production discipline.

modules.title: APIs and Enterprise Integrations
modules.intro: Forward deployed work lives or dies on connecting an AI system to the customer's real systems of record: CRMs, ERPs, ticketing tools, event buses and decades-old databases. This module covers the request/response contract (HTTP, JSON, OAuth 2.0), the push and streaming contract (webhooks and Kafka), and the patterns for integrating with and migrating off legacy systems without breaking the business.

modules.title: LLM Application Building Blocks
modules.intro: This module covers the four building blocks that almost every customer-facing LLM system is assembled from: the model API itself, the prompt and context around it, typed outputs and tools, and retrieval over private data. Each lesson starts from how the mechanism works and ends with how a deployed team operates it under real cost, latency and correctness constraints.

modules.title: Agents and Agentic Workflows
modules.intro: This module covers how agentic systems are designed, connected to customer systems, kept running through failures, measured, and constrained. It moves from single-agent loops and SDK primitives through MCP servers and durable orchestration to evaluation and guardrails, the parts that decide whether a deployment survives contact with production.

modules.title: Customer Data: Pipelines and Platforms
modules.intro: Customer deployments succeed or fail on the state of the customer's data: where it lives, how clean it is, and how reliably it moves. This module covers cleaning and linking messy records, working inside Snowflake and Databricks accounts you do not own, building tested transformations with dbt, and scheduling it all with Airflow or Dagster.

modules.title: Infrastructure and Deployment into Customer Environments
modules.intro: This module covers how an AI forward deployed engineer gets a system running inside infrastructure the customer owns: their cloud accounts, their clusters, their private networks and sometimes their GPUs. It moves from cloud and delivery fundamentals to restricted networks, self-hosted inference, and the latency and cost tradeoffs that decide whether a deployment survives production.

modules.title: Operating Deployments: Reliability, Security and Reuse
modules.intro: This module covers what happens after a deployment goes live: seeing what the system and its agents are doing, finding and fixing failures, and passing security and compliance review in regulated environments. It closes with how to turn the custom work of one engagement into platform features and internal tools that the next engagement can reuse.

steps.module: Foundations: The Forward Deployed Delivery Model
steps.why: A forward deployed engineer (FDE) is a software engineer embedded with a customer, responsible for making the product work on that customer's real data, systems and processes.

steps.module: Foundations: The Forward Deployed Delivery Model
steps.why: Scoping turns a customer's stated need into a bounded technical commitment, and the design document is where the trade-offs behind that commitment are written down and reviewed.

steps.module: Foundations: The Forward Deployed Delivery Model
steps.why: Before any model is called, an FDE has to understand how the customer's work is actually done and decide which steps are worth automating.

steps.module: Foundations: The Forward Deployed Delivery Model
steps.why: Prototypes, proofs of concept and pilots are how an FDE reduces uncertainty quickly and gives the customer evidence for a go or no-go decision.
Python is the default language for field integration work because one language covers throwaway scripts, data transformation, HTTP services and the whole AI library ecosystem.
TypeScript adds a static, structural type system on top of JavaScript and compiles away to plain JavaScript that Node.js runs on a single-threaded event loop.
Customers judge an AI deployment by the screen their people use, so a forward deployed engineer is often expected to build that screen as well as the backend.
Almost every deployment ends up reading from or writing to a relational database, and Postgres is the one most often named.
Agentic coding tools read a repository, run commands, edit files and iterate on test results, which changes the engineer's job from typing code to directing and verifying it.
Most enterprise integrations are HTTP calls carrying JSON, authorized by an OAuth 2.0 access token.
Polling an API tells you what changed eventually; events tell you when it changes.
Customers buy AI systems to change how work is done, but the work still runs through systems that are old, poorly documented and business critical.
A large language model is a function that takes a sequence of tokens and predicts the next one, repeated until a stop condition.
Prompt engineering is the practice of writing instructions a model can follow reliably; context engineering is deciding what information occupies the window at each step and in what form.
Structured outputs make a model return data that conforms to a schema, so downstream code can consume it without parsing free text.
Retrieval-augmented generation supplies a model with relevant passages from an external corpus at request time, so answers are grounded in data the model was never trained on and can cite it.
An agentic system sits somewhere between a fixed workflow, where code decides the order of model calls, and an autonomous agent, where the model decides its next step in a loop with tools.
The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI applications to external systems, so one integration works across many hosts instead of being rewritten per agent framework.
Orchestration decides which agent or step runs next and what context it receives; durable execution makes sure a long run survives crashes, deploys and rate limits without losing or repeating work.
Evaluation turns a vague sense that the system seems fine into a number tied to defined success criteria, so prompts, models and architectures can be changed with evidence.
Responsible AI work combines a governance process that identifies and tracks risk with technical controls that limit what a model-driven system can see, say and do.
Customer data arrives as overlapping exports from CRMs, ERPs and spreadsheets, with inconsistent formats, missing values and the same real-world entity recorded many times.
Most enterprise customers already keep their analytical data in Snowflake or Databricks, so AI work starts inside an account someone else owns and governs.
In ELT, raw data is loaded into the warehouse first and transformed there with SQL.
An orchestrator schedules pipeline steps, runs them in dependency order, retries failures and records what happened.

steps.module: Infrastructure and Deployment into Customer Environments

steps.module: Infrastructure and Deployment into Customer Environments
steps.why: Many enterprise and government customers run workloads on networks with no public ingress, tightly filtered egress, or no internet connection at all.

steps.module: Infrastructure and Deployment into Customer Environments
steps.why: When a customer cannot or will not call a hosted model API, the forward deployed engineer has to run open-weight models on GPUs inside the customer environment.

steps.module: Infrastructure and Deployment into Customer Environments
steps.why: LLM systems have an unusual cost and latency profile: spend scales with tokens, latency scales mostly with output length, and capacity is bounded by provider rate limits or by GPUs.

steps.module: Operating Deployments: Reliability, Security and Reuse
steps.why: Observability is the ability to understand what a running system is doing from the telemetry it emits: logs, metrics and traces.

steps.module: Operating Deployments: Reliability, Security and Reuse
steps.why: Debugging production systems is a disciplined loop of triage, observation, hypothesis and test, not a hunt driven by intuition.

steps.module: Operating Deployments: Reliability, Security and Reuse
steps.why: Regulated customers will not put an AI system into production until it passes their security and compliance review.

steps.module: Operating Deployments: Reliability, Security and Reuse
steps.why: Forward deployed work creates custom solutions under time pressure, and its long-term value depends on how much of that work the next engagement can reuse.
